s: Which of the following is NOT correct about prohibited grounds of discrimination?
o: Descent is a prohibited ground under Article 15(1).
Caste and sex are prohibited grounds under Article 15(1).
Religion and race are prohibited grounds under Article 15(1).
Descent is a prohibited ground under Article 16(2).
x: Article 15(1) covers only religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth; descent appears in Article 16(2).

s: A private hotel refuses entry to a person solely on the ground of caste. Which constitutional provision is most directly attracted?
x: Article 15(2) applies to access to places such as hotels and binds private persons as well as the State. It prohibits discrimination on the specified grounds in such access.

s: Under Article 16(3), who may prescribe residence requirements for certain public employment?
x: Article 16(3) permits Parliament to prescribe residence requirements; Article 16(2) lists descent and residence among prohibited grounds.

s: Article 16(5) permits a qualification relating to religion or denomination for an office connected with which of the following?
o: Every public employment under a State
x: Article 16(5) permits offices connected with religious or denominational institutions to be kept for persons professing that particular religion or belonging to that denomination.

s: To whom is Article 16, on equality of opportunity in public employment, available?
x: Articles 15 and 16 are available to citizens only; Article 14 alone extends to all persons.

s: Under which Article are 'descent' and 'residence' barred grounds of discrimination?
x: Article 16(2) adds descent and residence to the barred grounds; Article 15(1) lists only religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth.

s: Which Article of the Constitution provides that 'there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State'?
x: Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment to all citizens.

s: Which Article guarantees general equality of opportunity in public employment?
x: Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in public jobs; 16(4) covers reservation and 15(5) educational advancement.

s: Under which Article is the carry-forward of backlog reserved vacancies provided?
x: Article 16(4B) deals with backlog vacancies; 16(4A) concerns reservation in promotion for SCs and STs with consequential seniority.

s: Which Amendment inserted Article 15(5), enabling reservation in admission to private aided or unaided educational institutions?
x: Article 15(5) came with the 93rd Amendment (2005) and excludes minority institutions under Article 30; the 1st inserted 15(4), the 77th 16(4A) and the 103rd 15(6)/16(6).

s: Which power of the States was restored by the 105th Constitutional Amendment (2021)?
o: Exceed the 50 per cent reservation ceiling
Specify the Central List of SEBCs
Identify socially and educationally backward classes
Abolish the Central List of SEBCs
x: The 105th Amendment reversed the Maratha-case reading of the 102nd Amendment and restored the States' power to identify SEBCs.

s: Under which Article does the National Commission for Backward Classes have constitutional status?
x: The National Commission for Backward Classes is a constitutional body under Article 338B.

s: Which pair of clauses relates specifically to SCs, STs or OBCs?
x: Articles 15(4) and 16(4) concern SCs, STs or OBCs; Article 29 protects the cultural and educational rights of any section.

s: Which group lies outside the special provisions specifically described under Article 15?
x: Article 15 special provisions cover women, children, SEBCs, SCs, STs and, under 15(6), EWS; aged persons are not included.

s: Under Article 342A, who specifies the Central List of SEBCs?
x: Article 342A provides for the President to specify SEBCs for the Central List, while States retain their own lists.

s: Which Article provides for special provisions for women and children?
x: Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women and children. Article 15(4) covers SCs, STs and OBCs, and 15(5) the educational advancement of weaker sections.

s: Which Amendment inserted Article 16(4B) on carried-forward backlog vacancies?
x: The 81st Amendment (2000) inserted 16(4B), treating backlog vacancies as a separate group outside the 50% ceiling.

s: Which Amendment added consequential seniority for SC/ST promotions under Article 16(4A)?
x: The 77th Amendment (1995) gave promotion reservation; the 85th (2001) added consequential seniority, nullifying the catch-up rule.

s: Which Amendment first provided reservation in promotion for SCs and STs under Article 16(4A)?
x: The 77th Amendment (1995) inserted 16(4A) on SC/ST promotions, undoing Indra Sawhney on promotions.

s: To which of the following does reservation in admissions under Article 15(5) NOT apply?
x: Article 15(5) covers admissions including private aided or unaided institutions but excludes Article 30 minority institutions.

s:
Consider the following statements about the 103rd Constitutional Amendment:
1. It inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
2. It was passed in the Lok Sabha as the 124th Amendment Bill.
3. It provides EWS reservation of up to 27%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The EWS quota is up to 10%; 27% is the OBC quota upheld in Indra Sawhney.

s: Which Amendment gave the National Commission for Backward Classes constitutional status under Article 338B?
x: The 102nd Amendment made the NCBC a constitutional body under Article 338B.

s: What do Articles 15(6) and 16(6), inserted by the 103rd Constitutional Amendment, 2019, relate to?
o: Reservation for SCs and STs in promotions only
Reservation for EWS up to 10 per cent
x: The 103rd Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), providing for reservation for Economically Weaker Sections up to 10 per cent. It was passed as the 124th Amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha.

s: Under which Article does the President appoint a commission to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes?
x: Article 340 lets the President appoint a commission on the conditions of SEBCs; 338B is the NCBC and 342A the Central List.

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 14 and 15?
o: Article 14 applies to all persons, whereas Article 15 is available only to citizens.
Article 14 applies only to citizens, whereas Article 15 applies to all persons.
Both Articles 14 and 15 are available only to citizens.
Both Articles 14 and 15 apply only to foreigners residing in India.
x: Article 14 applies to any person within the territory of India. Article 15 is a right available only to citizens.

s: What does Article 17 of the Constitution deal with?
o: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion and race
Equality of opportunity in public employment
x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence.

s: Which distinctions are excepted from the bar on titles under Article 18(1)?
x: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring any title except military and academic distinctions.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 16 – Equality of opportunity in public employment
x: Article 16 deals with equal opportunity in public employment; Article 14 is equality before law, 15 prohibition of discrimination and 18 abolition of titles.

s: Which Article prohibits human trafficking?
x: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour. Article 24 bans child labour, 21A gives the right to education, and 25 freedom of religion.

s: Which Article provides the right of minorities to establish educational institutions?
x: Article 30 concerns minority educational institutions; Article 29 protects cultural and educational rights.

s: What is the origin of the concept of 'equality before law'?
x: Equality before law is British and negative in nature; equal protection of the laws is American and positive.

s: What kind of concept is 'equal protection of the laws' under Article 14?
x: Equal protection is American in origin and positive (like treated alike); equality before law is British and negative.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court state that ‘equality is antithetic to arbitrariness’ or that equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies?
o: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
x: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) established the close constitutional relationship between equality and non-arbitrariness.

s: Which one of the following propositions is associated with Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) in the context of Article 14?
o: Class legislation is always valid if enacted by Parliament
Any arbitrary State action violates Article 14
Article 14 applies only to taxation laws
x: Maneka Gandhi reinforced the principle that arbitrary State action is inconsistent with Article 14. Unguided discretionary power may therefore be struck down.

s: A law creates two groups for different treatment. For the classification to be valid under Article 14, which combination is required?
o: Intelligible differentia and rational nexus with the object of the law
x: The twin test of reasonable classification is an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons or things and a rational nexus between the differentia and the object sought to be achieved.

s: In April 2026, on which benefit did the Supreme Court hold that the State cannot arbitrarily treat pensioners differently from serving employees?
x: The ruling held that pensioners cannot be treated differently from serving employees on dearness allowance without a classification valid under Article 14.

s: Which of the following does Article 14 permit?
x: Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the law's object.

s: In February 2026, the Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of which regulations in Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India?
x: In Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India (Feb 2026), the Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the UGC equity regulations.

s: How much prior notice is needed before a civil case can be instituted against the President or a Governor?
x: A civil case needs two months' prior notice, not six; criminal proceedings are barred during the term (Art. 361).

s: Which Article gives immunity for a true, non-malicious report of proceedings of Parliament or State legislatures?
x: Article 361A, inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978), protects true, non-malicious reports of legislative proceedings.

s: Which Article gives immunity to MPs for anything said or any vote given in the House?
x: Article 105 gives MPs this immunity; Article 194 does the same for MLAs.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 361?
o: The President and Governors are not answerable to courts
No criminal case lies against a Governor during the term
A criminal case may be started against the President during the term after two months' notice
A civil case may be instituted only after two months' notice
x: Article 361 bars criminal cases during the term altogether; the two months' notice applies only to civil cases.

s: Who among the following are immune from civil and criminal proceedings in India under international law?
o: Members of State Public Service Commissions
x: Under international law, foreign sovereigns, ambassadors, diplomats and UN agencies are immune from civil and criminal proceedings, an exception to equality before law.

s: By what name was the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 renamed by the 1976 amendment?
o: SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
x: The 1976 amendment renamed it the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, effective 19 November 1976.

s: Which year does the Protection of Civil Rights Act carry in its title?
x: The renamed Act keeps the year 1955; 1976 is only the year of the amendment that renamed it.

s: In which year was the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act enacted?
x: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 is a further law against caste atrocities.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 17:
1. The term 'untouchability' is defined in the Constitution.
2. Enforcing any disability arising from untouchability is an offence punishable by law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only statement 2 is correct; 'untouchability' is not defined in the Constitution.

s: Under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, which punishment is given to a person, not an SC/ST member, who fabricates false evidence so that an SC/ST member is convicted of a capital offence?
x: Section 3(2)(i) of the Act punishes such false evidence with imprisonment for life and fine.

s: Under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, what is the punishment if false evidence given by a non-SC/ST person leads to the conviction and execution of an innocent SC/ST member?
x: Section 3(2)(i) says that if an innocent SC/ST member is convicted and executed because of the false evidence, the person who gave it shall be punished with death.

s: Dicey opposed the idea that executive officials should be subject only to which of the following?
o: The ordinary law of the land
x: Dicey's second element puts everyone under the ordinary law and ordinary courts, so he opposed special tribunals for officials.

s: From which country did India borrow the concept of the Rule of Law?
x: The Rule of Law, set out by the British jurist A.V. Dicey (1885), came from Britain, like the Cabinet System and Parliamentary Government.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Dicey's third principle and India?
o: In the UK, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights
It concerns the primacy of individual rights
In India, the Constitution is the source of rights
x: India took Dicey's first two elements but reversed the third: in India rights flow from the Constitution, so it was not adopted unchanged.

s: Besides Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which case affirmed the Rule of Law as part of the Basic Structure?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
x: The Rule of Law was affirmed as a basic feature in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975).

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Dicey’s first element of Rule of Law?
o: No person can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner.
It requires the absolute supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power.
It recognises an inherent unlimited police power of the State.
x: Option C is incorrect: Dicey's first element, absence of arbitrary power, means regular law is supreme and no one is punished except for a breach of law. It rejects unlimited state power.

s: Which of the following is consistent with the Rule of Law?
o: The ruler remains above the law.
Executive discretion operates without objective standards.
Laws are valid whether or not they are fair.
x: Under the Rule of Law, government is bound by law and laws must be just and fair; a ruler above the law belongs to 'rule by law'.

s: The Rule of Law in India is anchored primarily in which Article?
x: The rule of law in India rests mainly on Article 14: equality before law and equal protection of the laws.

s: In which year was A.V. Dicey's 'Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution', which set out the Rule of Law, published?
x: Dicey, a British jurist, expounded the Rule of Law in his 1885 book.

s: What is a system called in which the ruler stays above the law and uses law as a weapon of state control?
x: Under Rule by Law the ruler is above the law; under Rule of Law the government is subordinate to law.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of Dicey's three classic elements of the Rule of Law?
o: Primacy of the rights of the individual
x: Dicey's elements are absence of arbitrary power, equality before law and primacy of individual rights; people's duty to government is not one.

s: Which element of Dicey's Rule of Law means that regular law is supreme and the powers of the Government are limited?
x: Dicey's first element, absence of arbitrary power, means regular law is supreme and limits government power; this idea of limited government is the core of constitutionalism.

s:
Assertion (A): Article 18 is associated with social equality.
Reason (R): It seeks to end artificial distinctions created through State-conferred titles.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true. Article 18 advances social equality by abolishing artificial distinctions arising from State-conferred titles, subject to the stated exceptions.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about titles under Article 18?
o: A non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State needs the President's consent to accept a foreign title.
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles under Article 18.
A holder of an office of profit or trust needs the President's consent to accept any present from a foreign State.
A citizen of India may accept a foreign title with the President's consent.
x: Under Art. 18(2) a citizen shall not accept a foreign title at all; there is no consent route.

s: In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), what did the Supreme Court hold about Bharat Ratna and Padma awards?
o: May be used as hereditary titles
Are not titles under Article 18, but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes
x: The Court held these awards are not titles under Article 18, but they cannot be used as prefixes or suffixes to a name.

s: A non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State needs whose consent to accept a foreign title?
x: Under Article 18(3), such a non-citizen needs the President's consent.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 18(3) – Non-citizen office-holder needs the President's consent for a foreign title
Article 18(1) – Citizen barred from accepting any foreign title
Article 18(2) – State confers no title except military or academic
Article 18(4) – Citizen may accept a foreign title with Parliament's consent
x: 18(3) is correctly matched; 18(1) bars State titles except military or academic, and 18(2) bars citizens from foreign titles.

s: Under Article 18(2), when may an Indian citizen accept a title from a foreign State?
x: Article 18(2) bars a citizen from accepting a foreign title at all; consent applies only under 18(3) and 18(4).

s: How did B. R. Ambedkar describe liberty, equality and fraternity?
o: Economic objectives confined to the Directive Principles
Three independent ideals applicable to separate institutions
Duties imposed only on public servants
x: Ambedkar described liberty, equality and fraternity as an inseparable trinity.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Articles 39(b), 39(c) and 39(d), which are Directive Principles, are associated with economic equality. Social equality is associated with Articles 15, 17 and 18.

s: Through which provisions is economic equality mainly secured in the Indian Constitution?
x: Economic equality rests on DPSP Article 39(b), (c), (d) and is not part of the fundamental right to equality.

s: Which Articles secure political equality - no exclusion from electoral rolls and adult suffrage?
x: Articles 325 and 326 secure political equality; 39(b)-(d) secure economic equality and 17-18 social equality.

s: Which kind of equality does the Preamble of the Constitution promise?
o: Equality of status and of opportunity
Equality of income and of wealth
Equality of property and of status
Equality of religion and of caste
x: The Preamble promises 'equality of status and of opportunity'.

s: What reservation quota for OBCs was upheld in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)?
x: Indra Sawhney upheld the 27% OBC quota, excluded the creamy layer and set a 50% ceiling.

s: Which Amendment introduced the 10% EWS quota upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India?
x: Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the 103rd Amendment's 10% EWS quota, accepting economic criteria alone as a valid basis.

s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. M.R. Balaji
B. Champakam Dorairajan
C. Indra Sawhney
D. M. Nagaraj
x: Champakam Dorairajan was decided in 1951, M.R. Balaji in 1962, Indra Sawhney in 1992 and M. Nagaraj in 2006, giving B, A, C, D.

s: Under which Article did the Supreme Court strike down the Communal Government Order in Champakam Dorairajan?
x: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Communal G.O. was struck down under Article 29(2). The case also established the then-prevailing position that Directive Principles were subordinate to Fundamental Rights, leading to the First Amendment and Article 15(4).

s: In which case, and by what majority, did the Supreme Court uphold the 103rd Constitutional Amendment providing reservation for Economically Weaker Sections?
x: In Janhit Abhiyan (2022), the Supreme Court upheld the 103rd Amendment providing 10 per cent EWS reservation by a 3:2 majority.

s: Which case held that caste cannot be the sole test of backwardness and that reservation should generally stay below 50%?
o: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
x: M.R. Balaji held that caste cannot be the sole test and reservation should generally remain below 50%, and must be reasonable.

s: The Supreme Court’s decision in Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021) primarily concerned which issue?
o: Validity of the Maratha reservation exceeding the 50 per cent ceiling
Validity of reservation for SC converts to Christianity
Exclusion of the creamy layer from EWS reservation
x: The Maratha quota was struck down for crossing the 50 per cent ceiling without exceptional circumstances.

s: What did the Champakam Dorairajan case concern?
o: Caste not being the sole test of backwardness
x: Champakam Dorairajan concerned the Madras Communal G.O.; M.R. Balaji dealt with caste as sole test and the 50% principle.

s: The First Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 15(4) primarily to overcome the effect of which judgment?
o: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
x: Article 15(4) was inserted by the First Amendment, 1951 in response to the ruling in Champakam Dorairajan, which had struck down the Communal G.O. under Article 29(2).

s: Which case required quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation and administrative efficiency for promotion reservation?
x: M. Nagaraj (2006) laid down the quantifiable data requirement; Indra Sawhney ruled out reservation in promotions.

s: Which of the following is NOT a recognised exception or qualification to the 50% reservation ceiling?
o: Carry-forward of backlog vacancies under the 81st Amendment
Extraordinary situations such as remote areas
Every reservation made by a State legislature, without limitation
EWS reservation upheld in Janhit Abhiyan
x: There is no unrestricted power for every State legislature to exceed the ceiling.

s: What is the Centre's current position on an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs?
o: Has left the matter entirely to the States
Supports it only for Scheduled Tribes
x: The current position is that the Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs.

s: In April 2026, with what did Andhra Pradesh align its OBC creamy-layer definition?
o: A separate, higher State income ceiling
x: Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy-layer definition and thresholds with the central income limits in April 2026.

s: Which case was overruled by the 7-judge bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)?
x: The 7-judge bench overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) and allowed sub-classification of SCs and STs based on empirical data.

s: Under which Article did M. Nagaraj require data on overall administrative efficiency for promotion reservation?
x: M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld promotion reservation for SCs and STs subject to data on backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency under Article 335.

s: Which of the following pairs of case and year is wrongly matched?
o: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta – 2006
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh – 1997
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India – 2006
State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh – 2024
x: Jarnail Singh was decided in 2018; 2006 is M. Nagaraj.

s: Which case held that tribal land cannot be leased to private parties or corporations?
o: Janki Prasad Parimoo v. State of J&K
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh
x: Samatha (1997) barred leasing tribal land to private parties or corporations; Janki Prasad Parimoo held caste alone cannot be the sole test of backwardness.

s: What is the OBC creamy-layer income limit under the 2017 notification?
x: The 2017 notification set the OBC creamy-layer limit at ₹8 lakh a year; Andhra Pradesh aligned with these central thresholds.

s: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India is associated with upholding which of the following amendments, subject to conditions?
x: M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld the 77th and 85th Constitutional Amendments concerning reservation in promotion, subject to specified constitutional conditions.

s: Which case removed the requirement to prove backwardness of SCs and STs for reservation in promotion?
o: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006)
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018)
State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)
x: Jarnail Singh (2018) removed the need to prove backwardness and extended the creamy layer to SC/ST promotions; Nagaraj had required quantifiable data.

s: In which case do the creamy layer exclusion and the 50% reservation ceiling originate?
x: Both the creamy layer and the 50% cap originate in Indra Sawhney (1992).

s: By what majority did the nine-judge bench decide Indra Sawhney (1992)?
x: The Mandal case was decided 6:3 by nine judges.

s: By what majority was State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), allowing sub-classification of SCs/STs, decided?
x: The seven-judge bench ruled 6:1 and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).

s: Which of the following pairs of case and holding is correctly matched?
o: Janki Prasad Parimoo – Upheld 10% EWS quota
Ashoka Kumar Thakur – Upheld the 93rd Amendment
x: Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) upheld the 93rd Amendment; Davinder Singh overruled E.V. Chinnaiah and the EWS quota was upheld in Janhit Abhiyan.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that there can be no reservation in promotions?
x: Indra Sawhney (1992) barred reservation in promotions; the 77th Amendment (1995) then inserted Article 16(4A).

s: In which case did the Supreme Court uphold the role of the Gram Sabha under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 in protecting the rights of the Dongria Kondh?
o: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh
Janki Prasad Parimoo v. State of J&K
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
x: In the Niyamgiri case (Orissa Mining Corp., 2013) the Court upheld the Gram Sabha's role under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and the Dongria Kondh's rights.

s: Which case extended the creamy layer principle to reservation in promotions for SCs and STs?
x: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) removed the need to prove SC/ST backwardness and extended the creamy layer to SC/ST promotions.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court order the setting up of a permanent body for backward classes, which led to the National Commission for Backward Classes?
x: Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld 27% OBC reservation and ordered a permanent body, the NCBC.

s: Which Article guarantees the right to reside and settle in any part of India?
x: Article 19(1)(e) guarantees the right to reside and settle; 19(1)(b) is assembly, 19(1)(d) movement and 19(1)(g) profession, trade or business.

s: Which Article earlier contained the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property, later deleted?
x: The property right belonged to Article 19(1)(f) and was later deleted; Article 19(1)(c) covers associations, unions and co-operative societies.

s: Co-operative societies were added to Article 19(1)(c) by which Constitutional Amendment?
x: The 97th Amendment (2011) added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c). The 44th deleted the Right to Property and the 86th added the Right to Education.

s: Without an Advisory Board's report, what is the maximum period of preventive detention under Article 22?
x: Article 22 limits preventive detention without an Advisory Board's report to three months.

s: Which Article provides protection in respect of conviction for offences?
x: Article 20 gives protection in respect of conviction; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, 22 protects against arrest and detention, and 19 lists the six freedoms.

s: The Ninety-seventh Amendment, 2011, relating to co-operative societies, is also associated with which provisions?
x: The amendment relating to co-operative societies is also associated with Article 43B and Part IXB.

s: How many freedoms did Article 19(1) originally guarantee?
x: Article 19(1) had seven freedoms; deletion of 19(1)(f) left six.

s: Which Amendment deleted the right to property under Article 19(1)(f)?
x: The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted 19(1)(f); the 97th added co-operative societies to 19(1)(c).

s: Which Articles of Part III make up the Right to Freedom group?
x: The Right to Freedom group is Articles 19-22; Article 14 belongs to the Equality group.

s: Which of the following is NOT a freedom guaranteed under Article 19(1)?
o: Freedom to reside and settle in any part of India
Freedom to move freely throughout India
x: Freedom of conscience is in Article 25, not Article 19(1); co-operative societies (19(1)(c)), residence (19(1)(e)) and movement (19(1)(d)) are Article 19 freedoms.

s: Which Article guarantees the freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India?
x: 19(1)(d) covers movement; 19(1)(e) residence and settlement.

s: Which right is not expressly listed in Article 19(1) but has been read into freedom of speech and expression?
x: Courts have read press freedom into Article 19(1)(a); there is no FR to strike, travel abroad is under Article 21 and 19(1)(f) was deleted.

s: With which case are telecast rights and the absence of a government monopoly over airwaves under Article 19(1)(a) associated?
x: Cricket Association of Bengal concerned telecast and the absence of a government monopoly over airwaves; PUCL is associated with safeguards against phone tapping.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
x: The right to information has been read into Article 19(1)(a). Travel abroad is associated with Article 21, the right to strike is not a Fundamental Right, and clause (f) relating to property has been deleted.

s: In which form is freedom of speech and expression protected under Article 19?
o: Only for oral speech in public places
Only in printed newspapers and books
Irrespective of the medium of communication
x: Article 19 protects expression irrespective of the medium, extended by courts to the press, television and the Internet, subject to lawful restrictions.

s: In which case was the right to silence (not singing the national anthem) read into Article 19(1)(a)?
x: Bijoe Emmanuel recognised the right to silence. Tata Press concerned commercial speech, Naveen Jindal flag hoisting and Anuradha Bhasin internet speech.

s: Which case recognised speech and trade over the internet as protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g)?
x: Anuradha Bhasin protected speech and trade over the internet and required internet shutdowns to be proportionate, temporary and published.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Bennett Coleman case – Section 66A of the IT Act struck down
Shreya Singhal case – Community standards test for obscenity
Naveen Jindal case – Flying the national flag as expression
Aveek Sarkar case – Newsprint policy fixing number of pages
x: Naveen Jindal recognised flying the national flag as expression under Article 19(1)(a); Bennett Coleman was on newsprint policy, Shreya Singhal struck down Section 66A and Aveek Sarkar adopted the community standards test.

s: Why may films be pre-censored in a way the press cannot?
o: Are regulated only by the States
x: Films are considered capable of reaching larger audiences, so they may be pre-censored where the press cannot; neither enjoys absolute protection.

s: In which case was commercial speech recognised as part of Article 19(1)(a)?
x: Tata Press (1995) protected commercial speech; Naveen Jindal is flag hoisting and Bijoe Emmanuel the right to silence.

s: In which case was the right to information read into freedom of speech?
o: State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975)
x: Raj Narain (1975) read the right to know into 19(1)(a); PUCL concerned phone tapping.

s: In which case was hoisting the National Flag, including on private buildings, held part of freedom of expression?
x: Naveen Jindal (2004) recognised hoisting the National Flag as part of 19(1)(a).

s: In which case did the Supreme Court lay down safeguards against phone tapping?
x: In PUCL (1997) the Supreme Court laid down safeguards against phone tapping, protecting free speech and privacy.

s: In which 1961 case did the Supreme Court protect freedom of the press, including its circulation, under Article 19(1)(a)?
x: Sakal Papers (1961) is one of the cases that read press freedom and circulation into Article 19(1)(a); Romesh Thappar was 1950 and Bennett Coleman 1972.

s: Which of the following is a ground for restricting the freedom of assembly under Article 19(3)?
x: Article 19(3) permits restrictions on assembly in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India and public order; morality and security of the State are not its grounds.

s: Under which Article is 'general public interest' a ground for reasonable restrictions?
x: General public interest is a ground under Article 19(5) but not under Article 19(2); sedition and economic grounds are not listed in Article 19(2).

s: Which Article permits prescribing professional or technical qualifications for an occupation?
x: Article 19(6) allows general public interest, professional or technical qualifications and State trade or monopoly; Scheduled Tribes' protection belongs to 19(5).

s: Which ground was added to Article 19(2) by the Sixteenth Amendment, 1963?
x: Sovereignty and integrity of India came with the Sixteenth Amendment, 1963; the other three grounds were added by the First Amendment, 1951.

s: Which Article provides reasonable restrictions on the freedom of assembly?
x: Article 19(3) concerns assembly; 19(2) covers speech, 19(5) movement and residence, and 19(6) profession, trade or business.

s: Under Article 19(5), besides the interests of the general public, on which ground may freedom of movement and residence be restricted?
o: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
x: Article 19(5) permits restrictions on Articles 19(1)(d) and (e) in the interests of the general public and to protect Scheduled Tribes.

s: Which clause permits the State to carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens, thereby allowing State monopolies?
x: Article 19(6) lets the State prescribe professional or technical qualifications and carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 19 provides eight grounds of reasonable restriction on freedom of speech and expression.
2. Freedom of peaceful assembly can be restricted in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India and public order.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
x: Article 19(2) lists eight grounds for restricting speech, and Article 19(3) permits restrictions on assembly for sovereignty and integrity and public order.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh (2023)?
o: Section 66A of the IT Act is valid subject to safeguards
Public order is not a ground under Article 19(2)
Flying the national flag is outside Article 19(1)(a)
The grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive
x: Kaushal Kishor held the Article 19(2) grounds exhaustive, so no extra restriction can be placed on ministers' speech; it also let Articles 19 and 21 be enforced against non-State actors.

s: The test for determining the reasonableness of restrictions on fundamental rights is particularly associated with which case?
o: Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
State of Madras v V.G. Row
Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
x: The reasonableness test, involving factors such as the nature of the right, the purpose and urgency of the restriction, and proportionality, is associated with V.G. Row (1952).

s: Which of the following is correct about reasonable restrictions under Article 19?
o: Once enacted in the public interest, a restriction cannot be reviewed by courts
Courts decide reasonableness, and a restriction must not eclipse the right
The purpose and urgency of a restriction need not be examined
x: Courts judge reasonableness by purpose, extent, urgency and proportionality, and a restriction must not eclipse the fundamental right itself.

s: The power of the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to create a State monopoly under Article 19(6) was inserted by which Amendment?
x: The First Amendment, 1951 rewrote Art. 19(6) and inserted the clause letting the State carry on any trade to the exclusion of citizens (State monopoly), shielding nationalisation. The 7th, 44th and 97th Amendments did not touch Art. 19(6); the 97th added co-operative societies to Art. 19(1)(c).

s: Which ground of restriction is found in Article 19(4) but NOT in Article 19(3)?
x: 19(4) allows sovereignty and integrity, public order and morality; 19(3) on assembly does not include morality.

s: Which Amendment added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence to Article 19(2)?
x: The 1st Amendment (1951) added these grounds; the 16th (1963) added sovereignty and integrity.

s:
Consider the following statements about the availability of Article 19:
1. A company, as a legal person, cannot claim Article 19.
2. Citizen shareholders of a company may sue for their Article 19 rights.
3. Kaushal Kishor (2023) held Articles 19 and 21 enforceable against non-State actors too.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: Article 19 is for citizens only, not companies, though citizen shareholders may sue, and Kaushal Kishor extended enforcement to non-State actors.

s: To whom are the freedoms guaranteed under Article 19 available?
o: Citizens and companies as legal persons
x: Article 19 rights are available only to citizens; foreigners cannot claim them and a company as a legal person cannot itself claim them.

s: A prisoner writes and publishes a book from jail. Which freedom is he using, which his detention does not take away?
x: A detained person loses freedom of movement but keeps freedom of expression, so he may write and publish books.

s: What does the expression 'golden triangle' in constitutional law refer to?
x: The Supreme Court's decision in Maneka Gandhi linked Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the constitutional golden triangle.

s: Which case is associated with linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the constitutional “golden triangle”?
x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) is identified with linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the golden triangle.

s: During a National Emergency, how does Article 358 suspend Article 19?
o: Only by a resolution of Parliament
Only after a Supreme Court order
x: Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically; Article 359 needs a Presidential order.

s: After the 44th Amendment, on which ground of emergency does Article 358 operate?
o: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
x: Since the 44th Amendment, Article 358 applies only to an emergency on war or external aggression, not armed rebellion.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Articles 358 and 359?
o: Articles 20 and 21 can be suspended under Article 359
Article 359 suspends only enforcement of the rights named
x: Since the 44th Amendment, Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Article 359.

s: The Centre has defended restrictions under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act in relation to associations by invoking which provision?
x: The Centre has invoked Article 19(4), which concerns reasonable restrictions on the freedom to form associations or unions, in defending FCRA curbs.

s: Which of the following is excluded from the freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b)?
x: Meetings, demonstrations and processions are protected when peaceful and unarmed; armed gatherings are excluded.

s: What is the status of the right to strike in India?
x: The right to strike is not a Fundamental Right; it is only a legal right. A gherao is also not protected as peaceful assembly.

s: Peaceful protest is a right of everybody, but which condition must a protest observe?
o: may occupy public space without restriction
is a Fundamental Right to strike
x: Peaceful protest is a right, but it cannot occupy public space without limitation or trouble other citizens.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that bandhs are illegal as they curb the freedoms of others?
x: CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar held bandhs illegal because they curb others' freedoms. Kameshwar Prasad protected demonstrations but not strikes, and T.K. Rangarajan denied government employees a right to strike.

s: Which case held that government employees have no right to strike?
x: T.K. Rangarajan (2003) denied government employees a right to strike; CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar held bandhs illegal.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in Kameshwar Prasad (1962)?
o: A strike is a fundamental right
A demonstration is protected but a strike is not
A gherao is a peaceful assembly
x: Kameshwar Prasad protected demonstrations but not strikes; bandhs are illegal and gherao is not peaceful assembly.

s: In INSAF (2020), which associations did the Supreme Court hold can be barred from receiving foreign contributions?
x: In INSAF (2020) the Court held that only associations in active politics are barred from foreign funds under the FCRA.

s: Which of the following is there no fundamental right to carry on under Article 19(1)(g)?
o: A lawful profession subject to reasonable regulation
A trade requiring prescribed technical qualifications
A dangerous or immoral trade such as trafficking
A lawful business subject to reasonable restrictions
x: No one has a right to carry on dangerous or immoral trades such as trafficking; lawful trades remain protected subject to reasonable restrictions.

s: Under which Article may entry and settlement of outsiders in Inner Line areas be limited to protect Scheduled Tribes?
x: Under 19(5), movement and residence may be restricted to protect Scheduled Tribes' culture, land and property.

s: In which case was the ban on the journal Cross Roads struck down, as 'public order' was then not an Article 19(2) ground?
o: Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
Bennett Coleman v Union of India
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar
x: Romesh Thappar (1950) struck down the Cross Roads ban; it contributed to the First Amendment, 1951.

s: In which case was Section 66A of the IT Act struck down as vague and overbroad?
x: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act.

s: In Bennett Coleman (1972), what did the Supreme Court hold violated press freedom?
o: A ban on the journal Cross Roads
A newsprint policy fixing the number of pages
x: Bennett Coleman struck down a newsprint policy fixing pages; Cross Roads was Romesh Thappar and 66A Shreya Singhal.

s: In Kedar Nath Singh (1962), in which situation was sedition under Section 124A IPC held valid?
x: Kedar Nath limited sedition to speech involving incitement to violence.

s: Which of the following pairs of case and ruling is correctly matched?
o: Anuradha Bhasin – Internet shutdowns must be proportionate, temporary and published
Shreya Singhal – Newsprint policy fixing pages struck down
Bennett Coleman – Section 66A of the IT Act struck down
Kedar Nath Singh – 'Community standards' test for obscenity
x: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) is correctly matched; the community standards test is from Aveek Sarkar (2014).

s: Which test for obscenity was laid down in Aveek Sarkar (2014)?
x: Aveek Sarkar (2014) judged obscenity by contemporary community standards.

s: Which law provides for the statutory Zero FIR?
x: The statutory Zero FIR is a BNSS provision, not a BNS one; BNS covers organised crime and mob lynching.

s: Which of the following pairs under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is correctly matched?
o: Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity – Section 196
x: Criminal defamation is Section 356 BNS; hate speech is Section 196 and acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity are Section 152.

s: An unlawful assembly of five or more persons, earlier under IPC Section 141, now falls under which section of the BNS?
x: Unlawful assembly moved from IPC s.141 to BNS s.189; s.163 of the BNSS covers prohibitory orders.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The BNS, 2023 replaced the IPC.
2. The BNSS, 2023 provides for a statutory Zero FIR.
3. The BNS, 2023 mandates video recording of search and seizure.
Which of the above statements are correct?
x: The BNS replaced the IPC and the BNSS brought in statutory Zero FIR; mandatory video recording of searches is in the BNSS, not the BNS.

s: Which section of the BNSS replaced Section 144 CrPC on prohibitory orders?
x: Prohibitory orders, earlier under Section 144 CrPC, are now under Section 163 BNSS.

s: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 deals with acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, in place of sedition?
x: Sedition (s.124A IPC) gave way to s.152 BNS on endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity; s.196 is hate speech and s.356 defamation.

s: The RTE Act, 2009 reserves what share of entry-level seats in unaided private schools for children of weaker groups?
x: The Act provides 25 per cent entry-level seats in unaided private schools for weaker groups; the provision does not apply to minority schools.

s: Under Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009, children of which age group get free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school?
x: Section 3 gives every child aged 6 to 14 years the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education is completed.

s: In which year was the right-to-education case Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka decided?
x: Mohini Jain was decided in 1992, followed by Unnikrishnan in 1993, the 86th Amendment in 2002 and the RTE Act in 2009.

s: Which of the following is NOT a change made by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002?
o: Inserted Article 21A for free and compulsory education of children aged 6 to 14
Changed Article 45 to provide early childhood care and education below 6 years
Added Article 51A(k), a duty of parents to provide education to children aged 6 to 14
Deleted the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights
x: The Right to Property was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978. The 86th Amendment changed Articles 21A, 45 and 51A(k).

s: What is the constitutional status of the Right to Education?
o: It is a Fundamental Duty of parents alone
It is only a Directive Principle of State Policy
It is a statutory right unrelated to Article 21
It is a Fundamental Right and is treated as an extension of the right to life
x: The Right to Education is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and is treated as an extension of the right to life under Article 21.

s: After the 86th Amendment, for children of which age does Article 45 provide early childhood care and education?
x: Article 45 now covers children below 6; Article 21A covers 6 to 14.

s: Up to what age did Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993) hold free education to be a right?
x: Unnikrishnan held free education a right up to 14; beyond that it depends on the State's economic capacity.

s:
Arrange in chronological order:
A. Mohini Jain v. Karnataka
B. 86th Amendment
C. Unnikrishnan v. State of AP
D. RTE Act
x: Mohini Jain (1992), Unnikrishnan (1993), 86th Amendment (2002), RTE Act (2009).

s: On which date did Article 21A and the RTE Act come into force?
x: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002), came into force with the RTE Act on 1 April 2010.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009?
o: Section 3 gives every child of 6-14 years free education in a neighbourhood school
25% of entry-level seats in unaided private schools are kept for weaker groups
The 25% quota applies to minority schools as well
Schools are reimbursed for the 25% seats
x: The 25% quota does not apply to minority schools; the other statements are correct.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 21 – Preventive detention and safeguards against arrest
Article 20 – Protection in respect of conviction for offences
Article 21A – Protection against ex post facto criminal laws
Article 22 – Free education for children aged six to fourteen
x: Article 20 protects in respect of conviction for offences; Article 21 covers life and liberty, 21A education and 22 arrest and detention.

s: To whom are the protections under Article 20 available?
o: Citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies
Natural persons present in India only
x: Article 20 protections extend to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies, subject to the nature of each protection.

s: To which laws does the protection under Article 20(1) against a heavier penalty apply?
x: Article 20(1) applies to criminal laws; it bars conviction and a greater penalty, but does not necessarily bar the trial itself.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about protection against double jeopardy?
o: Article 20(2) bars prosecution and punishment more than once for the same offence
The protection covers prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal
Article 20(2) also bars departmental proceedings after a criminal conviction for the same act
Section 337 BNSS replaces Section 300 CrPC as the corresponding provision
x: Article 20(2) covers only prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental proceedings.

s: In which case was it held that physical evidence such as fingerprints is not testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3)?
x: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) held that fingerprints and physical specimens are not testimonial self-incrimination; Article 20(3) covers oral and documentary testimony.

s: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that which of the following, when conducted without consent, violates Article 20(3)?
o: Verification of age through official records
x: Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).

s: Which Article provides protection from torture?
x: Prohibition against torture is not in Article 20; protection from torture is under Article 21.

s: Which clause of Article 20 bars ex post facto criminal laws?
x: Article 20(1) bars conviction under an ex post facto law; 20(2) is double jeopardy and 20(3) self-incrimination.

s: To whom is the protection under Article 21 available?
x: Article 21 protects citizens and non-citizens and has been read to include dignity, health and protection against solitary confinement.

s: In which case was the right to a clean environment and air read into Article 21?
x: Subhash Kumar recognised a clean environment; Parmanand Katara gave emergency medical aid, Olga Tellis shelter and livelihood, and Maneka Gandhi travel abroad.

s: In which case was emergency medical care read into Article 21?
x: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity concerned emergency medical care; Shafin Jahan is marriage by choice, Hoskot free legal aid, Hussainara speedy trial.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in Supriyo Chakraborty (2023)?
o: There is an unqualified fundamental right to marry
The right to privacy is unconstitutional
Travel abroad is not protected under Article 21
There is no fundamental right to marry as such
x: The Court held there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such, while Article 21 protection for dignity, privacy and choice of partner remains.

s: With which case is compensation for violation of human rights under Article 21 associated?
x: Nilabati Behera (1993) is associated with compensation for human rights violations; Puttaswamy recognised privacy.

s: In which case was the right to speedy trial read into Article 21?
x: Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial; Maneka Gandhi gave fair procedure, M.H. Hoskot free legal aid and Francis Coralie Mullin human dignity.

s: In which case was the right to livelihood read into Article 21?
x: Olga Tellis (1985) recognised livelihood; Chameli Singh shelter, Subhash Kumar clean environment.

s: In which case was the right to marry a person of one's choice under Article 21 upheld?
o: Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006)
x: Lata Singh (2006), followed by Shafin Jahan (2018), upheld marriage by choice under Article 21.

s: With which case is the right to live with human dignity under Article 21 associated?
x: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) read human dignity into Article 21; Hoskot is free legal aid.

s: In which case was free legal aid read into Article 21?
x: M.H. Hoskot (1978) read the right to free legal aid into Article 21.

s: In which 1989 case did the Supreme Court read the right to emergency medical aid into Article 21?
x: Parmanand Katara (1989) read the right to emergency medical aid into Article 21.

s: With which case is the right to shelter under Article 21 associated?
x: Chameli Singh (1995) recognised the right to shelter under Article 21.

s: Besides Maneka Gandhi (1978), which earlier case is linked with the right to travel abroad as part of personal liberty?
x: Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) are the cases on the right to travel abroad.

s: How many judges delivered the Puttaswamy (2017) judgment on privacy?
x: A nine-judge bench unanimously (9:0) held privacy a fundamental right.

s: Which cases did Puttaswamy (2017) overrule to the extent they denied privacy as a fundamental right?
x: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh; Govind and Malak Singh had read privacy into Article 21.

s:
Consider the following statements about the right to privacy:
1. It is protected mainly under Article 21.
2. Puttaswamy (2017) recognised it unanimously.
3. A limit on privacy must meet legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: privacy is under Article 21, Puttaswamy was 9:0, and its test is legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.

s: Preventive detention is constitutionally justified under Article 22 in relation to which of the following?
o: Mere law and order in every local dispute
Any administrative inconvenience caused by an individual
Public order, but not merely routine law and order
Only a civil disagreement between private parties
x: The Supreme Court has distinguished public order from ordinary law and order. Preventive detention cannot be justified merely by routine law-and-order concerns.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2)?
o: An arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours
The safeguards also cover a civil arrest and the deportation of an alien
The 24 hours exclude the time of journey
The safeguards are not available to an enemy alien or a preventive detainee
x: Arrest under court orders, civil arrest and deportation of aliens fall outside these safeguards; Article 22(3) also excludes enemy aliens and preventive detainees.

s: Under Article 22(1), what right does a person arrested and detained in custody have?
o: Be informed of the grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice
Be released on bail as of right within 24 hours
Be tried only by a jury
Have the case reviewed by an Advisory Board within three months
x: Art. 22(1) gives the right to be told the grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice (now Secs. 47 and 58 BNSS for the procedure). Bail as of right and trial by jury are not guaranteed, and the Advisory Board review belongs to preventive detention under Art. 22(4).

s: In Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025), the Supreme Court emphasised which of the following?
o: The grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee
The right to education is available only to citizens
Preventive detention can be ordered only after conviction
An Advisory Board must review every arrest within 24 hours
x: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana emphasised that the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.

s: Who are excluded by Article 22(3) from the safeguards of Articles 22(1) and 22(2)?
o: Enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention
x: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and preventive detainees.

s: Which of the following is NOT guaranteed to an arrested person under Article 22?
o: Being told the grounds of arrest
Production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours
x: Article 22 does not guarantee bail as of right or trial by jury.

s: Within how many hours must an arrested person be produced before the nearest magistrate?
x: Article 22(2) requires production within 24 hours, excluding journey time.

s: In bail cases under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, what has the Supreme Court said about delay alone?
o: not a trump card for granting bail
sufficient to invalidate the detention order
x: The Supreme Court observed on 6 January 2026 that delay alone is not a “trump card” for bail in UAPA cases.

s: What is meant by preventive detention?
o: After conviction, to execute a sentence
Ordered by a criminal court after a finding of guilt
Only for non-payment of a civil debt
Without trial, on suspicion of future harmful acts
x: Preventive detention is detention without trial based on apprehension of future harmful acts; punitive detention follows conviction.

s: Under Article 22(7), who may prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention?
x: Article 22(7) permits Parliament to prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention; Article 22(5) requires grounds and an opportunity of representation.

s: To what period did the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 seek to cut preventive detention without an Advisory Board report?
x: The 44th Amendment cut it from three to two months, but the clause was never notified, so three months still applies under Article 22(4).

s: On which matters can Parliament alone make preventive detention laws?
o: Defence, foreign affairs and security of India
x: Parliament alone legislates on preventive detention for defence, foreign affairs and security of India; Parliament and the States share public order, security of a State and essential supplies.

s: In which year was the National Security Act enacted?
x: The National Security Act came in 1980, after the Preventive Detention Act (1950), MISA (1971) and COFEPOSA (1974).

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: COFEPOSA, 1974 – Detention up to 12 months without charges
COFEPOSA, 1974 – Detention of suspected smugglers and currency manipulators
x: COFEPOSA targets smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators; NSA allows detention up to 12 months without charges and UAPA is the anti-terror law.

s: Who make up the Advisory Board under Article 22(4)?
o: High Court judges or persons qualified to be such judges
x: The Advisory Board is made of HC judges or persons qualified to be HC judges.

s: Under the National Security Act, for how long may a person be detained without charges?
x: The NSA (1980) allows detention up to 12 months without charges.

s: What was the first preventive detention law of independent India?
x: The Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was the first; it lapsed in 1969.

s: Which of the following pairs of law and year is correctly matched?
x: MISA was 1971; UAPA 1967, NSA 1980 and COFEPOSA 1974.

s: Which preventive detention law, enacted in 1971, was used during the Emergency and repealed in 1978?
x: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 was used in the Emergency and repealed in 1978.

s: Which clause of Article 22 requires that a detenu be told the grounds of detention and given the earliest opportunity of making a representation?
x: Article 22(5) requires the grounds to be communicated and the earliest opportunity of representation.

s: The expression 'procedure established by law' is taken from the constitution of which country?
x: 'Procedure established by law' is associated with Japan, while 'due process' is associated with the United States.

s: Unlike A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 also protects against which of the following?
x: A.K. Gopalan read Article 21 narrowly without testing legislation for fairness; Maneka Gandhi extended protection against arbitrary legislative action.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 21?
o: Article 21 uses the expression 'procedure established by law'
A.K. Gopalan (1950) held a law valid if enacted through correct legislative procedure
After Maneka Gandhi (1978), a law must also be just, fair and reasonable
After Maneka Gandhi (1978), any procedure enacted by the legislature suffices
x: Maneka Gandhi required the procedure to be just, fair and reasonable, so mere legislative enactment no longer suffices.

s: Which Article is violated by an unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power conferred on an executive authority?
x: Such discretion is arbitrary and subverts the Rule of Law, so it violates Article 14.

s: Which case treated Articles 19, 21 and 22 as separate provisions?
x: Gopalan kept Articles 19, 21 and 22 separate; Maneka Gandhi linked 14, 19 and 21 as the golden triangle.

s: Which legal maxim expresses the 'right to be heard', a core part of natural justice?
x: Audi alteram partem means 'hear the other side'; due process of law is in essence the principle of natural justice.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 21 uses the expression 'due process of law'.
2. Capital punishment is not barred by Article 21.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law', not 'due process'; capital punishment is not barred by Article 21.

s: In which year did the Supreme Court decide Common Cause, upholding the living will?
x: Common Cause was decided in 2018, after P. Rathinam (1994), Gian Kaur (1996) and Aruna Shanbaug (2011).

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Supreme Court rulings on the right to die?
o: P. Rathinam (1994) held Section 309 IPC unconstitutional
Aruna Shanbaug (2011) held the living will valid
Gian Kaur (1996) held there is no right to die and Section 309 IPC is valid
Common Cause (2018) upheld the living will / advance directive
x: Aruna Shanbaug allowed passive euthanasia under High Court supervision; it was Common Cause (2018) that upheld the living will.

s: Which of the following is correct about attempted suicide in India?
o: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 made it a general offence
The BNS retains Section 309 IPC unchanged
It was decriminalised in effect in 2017, and the BNS has no general offence for it
The BNS decriminalised every act intended to compel a public servant
x: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect, and the BNS (in force from 1 July 2024) has no general offence of attempted suicide.

s: From which date did the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replace the Indian Penal Code?
x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. It does not retain a general offence of attempted suicide corresponding to Section 309 IPC.

s: Which case declared Section 309 IPC (attempted suicide) unconstitutional?
x: P. Rathinam (1994) struck down Section 309; Gian Kaur (1996) overruled it and restored the section.

s: In which case was passive euthanasia under High Court supervision allowed?
x: Aruna Shanbaug (2011) rejected the plea but allowed passive euthanasia under HC supervision; Common Cause upheld the living will.

s: Which High Court held in Chenna Jagadeeswar (1988) that Article 21 gives no right to die and upheld Section 309 IPC?
x: In Chenna Jagadeeswar v. State of AP (1988), the Andhra Pradesh High Court upheld Section 309 IPC; the Bombay High Court took the opposite view in Maruti Dubal (1987).

s: Which High Court held in Maruti Shripati Dubal (1987) that the right to die is part of Article 21?
x: The Bombay High Court in Maruti Shripati Dubal (1987) held the right to die part of Article 21 and Section 309 IPC unconstitutional.

s: Since the 44th Amendment, the enforcement of which Articles can never be suspended under Article 359?
x: The 44th Amendment (1978) made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even in a National Emergency.

s: Which Amendment made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable during a National Emergency?
x: The 44th Amendment (1978) barred suspension of Articles 20 and 21 under Article 359; Puttaswamy reaffirmed this.

s: To whom, and against whom, is the protection against trafficking and forced labour under Article 23 available?
o: Only to Indian citizens and only against the State
To citizens and non-citizens, and against both the State and private persons
Only to persons employed in government institutions
Only when the exploitation is committed by a public authority
x: Article 23 protects both citizens and non-citizens and operates against the State as well as private persons.

s: In which kinds of work does Article 24 prohibit the employment of children below fourteen years?
o: Factories, mines and other hazardous employment
x: Article 24 bars employment of children below fourteen in factories, mines and other hazardous employment; harmless or innocent work is not covered.

s: Under the Child Labour Amendment Act, 2016, what is the position of adolescents aged 14-18 years?
o: Free to work in any occupation
Barred only from work in mines
x: The 2016 amendment bars adolescents aged 14–18 from hazardous work, and bars children below 14 from work except helping family after school.

s: Under which Article is compulsory service for a public purpose permitted as an exception?
x: Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; Article 23(2) is the exception for compulsory public service without discrimination.

s: What does 'Begar' mean in the context of Article 23?
o: Voluntary community service performed for religious purposes
Unpaid forced labour exacted by officials or zamindars
Paid labour performed under a written contract
Compulsory military service with regular remuneration
x: Begar refers to unpaid forced labour traditionally exacted by officials or zamindars.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 23(2)?
o: The State may impose compulsory service for public purposes
Such service may include military or social service
The State cannot discriminate solely on grounds of religion, race, caste or class in imposing it
The State must pay remuneration in every case of compulsory service
x: Article 23(2) does not require payment in every case of compulsory public service.

s: Which Directive Principles direct the State to ensure that the tender age of children is not abused and that children are protected against exploitation?
x: Articles 39(e) and 39(f) protect children's tender age from abuse and ensure healthy development with protection against exploitation.

s: In which year was the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, which abolishes debt bondage, enacted?
x: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act is of 1976; ITPA is of 1956 and the Child Labour Act of 1986.

s: Trafficking is dealt with under which Section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
x: Section 143 of the BNS, which replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024, deals with trafficking; victim consent is immaterial.

s: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and the State Commissions (SCPCRs) are constituted under which law?
o: Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
x: NCPCR and SCPCRs are set up under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005. POCSO 2012 deals with sexual offences against children, ITPA 1956 with brothels and immoral traffic, and the 1986 Act with child labour; none of them creates the commissions.

s: In which year was the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act enacted?
x: The ITPA dates from 1956; the Bonded Labour Act is of 1976 and the Child Labour Act of 1986.

s: In which year was the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act enacted?
x: The Child Labour Act is of 1986; its 2016 amendment renamed it the Child and Adolescent Labour Act.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 24?
o: It prohibits employing children below 14 in factories
It is enforceable against private individuals too
It covers mines and other hazardous employment
It bars even harmless or innocent work by children
x: Article 24 is an absolute prohibition on hazardous work, but harmless or innocent work is not barred.

s: While imposing compulsory service under Article 23(2), on which grounds may the State not discriminate?
x: Article 23(2) allows compulsory service for public purposes but bars discrimination on religion, race, caste or class.

s: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what is the legal value of a trafficking victim's consent?
x: Under Section 143 BNS, which replaced IPC 370, the victim's consent is immaterial.

s: Which two Articles together make the right against exploitation meaningful for children by giving them education and barring hazardous work?
x: Article 21A gives free education to children of 6-14 years and Article 24 bars children below 14 from hazardous work.

s: In which year was the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act enacted?
x: POCSO, on sexual offences against children, was enacted in 2012.

s: By its 2016 amendment, what was the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 renamed?
o: Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act
x: The 2016 amendment renamed it the Child and Adolescent Labour Act, banning children below 14 and barring adolescents of 14-18 from hazardous work.

s: How is the Right to Freedom of Religion under Articles 25 to 28 classified?
x: The freedoms guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 constitute Fundamental Rights and are not merely legal rights or Directive Principles.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the terms in Article 25(1)?
o: Worship, rituals and ceremonies integral to the religion fall under 'practise'
The freedom to follow no religion falls under 'conscience'
Wearing a turban, crucifix or kirpan is an instance of 'profess'
'Propagate' means the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God
x: Propagate means spreading one's beliefs to others; the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God is conscience.

s: Besides public order, morality and health, to what are the freedoms in Article 25(1) subject?
o: The other provisions of Part III
x: Article 25(1) expressly subjects these freedoms to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 25(2)?
o: 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religion
25(2)(b) lets the State provide for social welfare and reform
25(2)(b) lets the State throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes of Hindus
25(2)(a) lets the State regulate only spiritual beliefs, not secular activities
x: Article 25(2)(a) reaches secular activity associated with religion, not spiritual belief.

s: What may the State do where a religious practice involves a social evil?
o: Can never intervene in religious matters
Must leave reform entirely to the religious denomination
May intervene to root it out, subject to constitutional limits
x: Freedom of religion is not absolute; the State can intervene to root out social evils while respecting constitutional restrictions.

s: Propagation under Article 25 does not include a right to convert another person, because it would affect which right of the other person?
x: Propagation means spreading one's beliefs; a right to convert another would impinge on that person's freedom of conscience.

s: Which of the following does freedom of conscience under Article 25 include?
o: Carry on secular activity free of regulation
x: Conscience includes the freedom to follow no religion; propagation does not include a right to convert another.

s: For Article 25(2)(b), who are included in the expression 'Hindus'?
x: The explanation to Article 25 includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists within 'Hindus'; another explanation deems wearing kirpans part of the profession of Sikhism.

s: Under Article 25(2)(a), the State may regulate which activity associated with religion?
o: Economic, financial or political secular activity
x: Article 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate secular activities linked to religion, not spiritual belief.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that prisoners do not lose their Fundamental Rights merely because of lawful detention?
x: Sunil Batra held that Fundamental Rights survive custody, so a prisoner keeps freedoms such as freedom of religion.

s: Which one of the following is a characteristic of a theocratic state?
o: The Constitution prohibits any relationship between religion and public policy
Religious practices are entirely outside constitutional regulation
The State has no religion and treats all religions equally
An official religion guides law and State policy
x: A theocratic or religious state has an official religion that guides its law and State policy. Such a system is not a feature of the Indian Constitution.

s: Which case widened Section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
x: Abhiram Singh (2017) widened Section 123(3) RPA; Bommai (1994) made secularism a basic feature.

s: What is the status of Hindi under Article 343?
o: The official language of the Union
One of several equal official languages of the Union
The official language of every State
x: Article 343 makes Hindi the official language of the Union; India has no national language.

s: Which one of the following most appropriately describes the constitutional meaning of secularism in India?
o: Complete exclusion of religion from public life
Preference to the religion followed by the majority
Establishment of one official religion by the State
Equal respect for all religions and absence of discrimination on religious grounds
x: Indian secularism requires equal respect for all religions and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion. It does not establish a state religion or demand complete exclusion of religion from public life.

s: Which of the following describes Indian secularism?
o: A state religion with tolerance of other faiths
A strict bar on all state aid to religious institutions
No state religion, with positive state intervention for reform
Complete non-interference by the State in religion
x: India has no state religion and allows positive state intervention for social and religious reform; state aid to religious institutions is not necessarily barred.

s: Unlike the Western model of strict separation, on what is Indian secularism based?
o: A ban on state aid to religious institutions in all cases
Mutual exclusion of State and religion
x: The Western model rests on strict separation and mutual exclusion, while the Indian model adopts principled distance, equal respect and scope for reform.

s: The Constituent Assembly, in 1949, rejected the proposal to include which word in the Preamble?
x: The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to add the word “God” to the Preamble in 1949.

s: In which year was the Karachi Resolution, a root of Indian secular thought, adopted?
x: The Karachi Resolution (1931), with Ashoka's Dhamma and the Nehru Report (1928), is a root of Indian secular thought.

s: Which Article prevents exclusion of a person from electoral rolls on grounds including religion?
x: Article 325 prevents exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds including religion; it does not authorise such exclusion.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India – Secularism as a basic feature of the Constitution
Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen – Appeals on religion, race, caste, community or language as corrupt practice
Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police – Limits on indefinite occupation of public ways by protest
Shakti Vahini v. Union of India – Peaceful protest, subject to not occupying public ways indefinitely
x: Shakti Vahini protected the right to choose a life partner under Article 21; the limit on protest occupation came from Amit Sahni.

s: Which Amendment added the word 'Secular' to the Preamble?
x: The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted 'Secular'; Bommai held secularism was present even before.

s: Which case held secularism to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution?
x: S.R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure, inherent even before the 42nd Amendment. Maneka Gandhi concerned Article 21, Minerva Mills the limits of amending power and the FR-DPSP balance, and Golaknath the unamendability of Fundamental Rights.

s: Sarva Dharma Sambhava in Indian secularism combines state neutrality with what?
o: A ban on all state aid
Strict separation of religion and State
x: Sarva Dharma Sambhava means state neutrality plus positive intervention for reform, unlike Western strict separation.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold khap interference in marriages and honour killings to be illegal?
x: Shakti Vahini (2018) held khap interference and honour killings illegal; choice of partner is part of Article 21.

s: According to S.R. Bommai (1994), under which Article can a State Government acting against secularism be dismissed?
x: Bommai held secularism a basic feature and said anti-secular State governments can be dismissed under Article 356.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Article 28 – Freedom from taxes for promotion of a particular religion
Article 24 – Prohibition of employment of children below 14 in hazardous employment
Article 25 – Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
Article 26 – Right of a religious denomination to manage its religious affairs
x: Freedom from taxes for promoting a particular religion is Article 27; Article 28 concerns religious instruction or worship in certain institutions.

s: Which right do Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution together form?
x: Articles 23–24 form the Right against Exploitation, and Articles 25–28 the Right to Freedom of Religion.

s: To whom is the right under Article 27 available?
